title: Before the King, and by Night Around the Walls
summary: Four months after hearing the news, Nehemiah serves wine to Artaxerxes with a sad face, and the king asks why. With a silent prayer, Nehemiah asks to be sent to rebuild the city of his fathers, and the king grants him leave, letters of safe passage, timber, and an armed escort. In Jerusalem Nehemiah inspects the ruined walls secretly by night, then calls the leaders to rebuild, and they agree, while Sanballat, Tobiah, and Geshem mock and accuse them of rebellion.
story: Chapter 1 ended with Nehemiah praying for success before this man. Chapter 2 shows the prayer answered, though not without risk. The chapter moves from the palace in Susa to the ruined city in Jerusalem, and it introduces the pattern the next five chapters will follow: God's gracious hand opens the way, Nehemiah plans carefully, the people take up the work, and enemies respond with contempt and threats. It also introduces the three opponents who will shadow the whole project. The call in verse 17 to rebuild the wall so that we will no longer be a disgrace sets up chapter 3, where the people divide the work and begin.
historical:
Nisan (March to April) of Artaxerxes' twentieth year was the spring of 445 BC, about four months after Nehemiah first heard the news. The king had earlier ordered work on Jerusalem's walls stopped until he gave further order (Ezra 4:21), so Nehemiah was in effect asking him to reverse his own decision, which helps explain Nehemiah's fear. The letters he requested were the standard documents of Persian travel and administration, and the escort of army officers and cavalry fits the status of a royal appointee; 5:14 reveals that he had been made governor of Judah.

Nehemiah's opponents were significant figures. Sanballat is named in the Elephantine papyri of about 407 BC as governor of Samaria, the province to the north, whose sons were by then acting for him. Horonite probably links him to Beth-horon, a town northwest of Jerusalem, or to Horonaim in Moab. Tobiah, called the Ammonite official, likely held authority in the region east of the Jordan; a family known as the Tobiads was prominent there in later centuries, and many scholars connect him with it. Geshem the Arab is probably the Gashmu known as the father of Qaynu, king of Qedar, from an inscribed silver bowl found at Tell el-Maskhuta in Egypt. Qedar was a powerful Arab kingdom controlling trade routes to the south and east. A rebuilt Jerusalem threatened the influence all three held over Judah.
cultural:
At the Persian court, showing sorrow in the king's presence could be dangerous, since the king's company was supposed to be a place of joy, and a gloomy servant might be suspected of discontent or plotting. That is why Nehemiah was overwhelmed with fear when the king noticed his face. His answer is shrewd: he speaks first of the place where his fathers are buried, appealing to the universal duty to honor ancestral graves, and does not name Jerusalem until later, a city the king had reason to suspect. He asks for timber from the king's forest (Hebrew pardes, a Persian loanword for an enclosed park or reserve, from which the English word paradise eventually comes).

Nehemiah's night inspection reflects both prudence and knowledge of local politics. He tells no one what he plans until he has seen the damage for himself. He rides out through the Valley Gate on the west, goes south to the Dung Gate, and turns up the eastern side past the Fountain Gate and the King's Pool, where rubble blocks his animal. Excavations on the eastern slope of the City of David, including those of Kathleen Kenyon in the 1960s, found collapsed stone terraces there, which fits the picture of a slope choked with debris.
literary: The chapter continues Nehemiah's first-person memoir and falls into two halves: the palace scene (verses 1-10) and the Jerusalem scene (verses 11-20). Each ends with the opponents' reaction (verses 10 and 19-20). The palace scene is told with close attention to feeling and timing: Nehemiah had never been sad before the king, he is afraid, and between the king's question and his own answer he prays to the God of heaven, a prayer the text reports in a single clause. The phrase the gracious hand of my God (verses 8 and 18), borrowed from Ezra 7-8, links Nehemiah's success to the same providence that guided Ezra. The chapter ends with Nehemiah's sharp reply to his opponents, which uses three legal terms: they have no portion, right, or claim in Jerusalem.

outline.t: Letters, timber, and the king's consent
Nehemiah travels to Judah, and opponents take notice
A secret inspection of the walls by night
The call to rebuild, and the people's response

doctrines.note: Between the king's question and his answer, Nehemiah prays to the God of heaven. After months of prayer, a quick silent prayer in the moment is enough. The chapter shows prayer as both long preparation and instant dependence.

The king grants everything because the gracious hand of God was upon Nehemiah. God works through a king's mood, a queen's presence, letters and timber, and Nehemiah's careful planning, all without a miracle.

Nehemiah tells the people what God had put in his heart and invites them into the work, and they strengthen their hands for it. God's purposes move forward through a shared calling, not one person's effort.

words.note: Cherpah, reproach or disgrace. Nehemiah calls the people to rebuild so that they will no longer be a disgrace (verse 17). In the ancient world a ruined city shamed its people and, for Israel, the God whose name was attached to Jerusalem. Rebuilding was a matter of honor, God's more than theirs.

Pardes, a park or forest, a loanword from Persian meaning an enclosed garden or reserve. Asaph is keeper of the king's pardes. The Greek form paradeisos was later used for the garden of Eden in the Greek Old Testament, and it gives English its word paradise.

Chazaq, to be strong or strengthen. In verse 18 the people strengthened their hands for the good work, that is, they took courage and set to it. The same verb will appear some thirty-five times in chapter 3 as the word for repairing the wall, so the strengthening of the people and of the wall go together.

Cheleq, a portion or share, especially an allotted inheritance. Nehemiah tells his opponents they have no portion, right, or claim in Jerusalem (verse 20). He uses the language of inheritance to deny them any legal or religious standing in the city of God.

christ: Nehemiah goes from the king's presence to a ruined city, sent with the king's authority to rebuild it and restore its people's honor. The New Testament does not treat Nehemiah as a prophecy of Christ, but the pattern resonates. Jesus is sent from the Father to the city that would reject him, and his work is described as building: he said he would build his church (Matthew 16:18), and the letters describe believers as built together into a dwelling place for God (Ephesians 2:22). Nehemiah's opponents mock and accuse him of rebellion against the king, much as Jesus' opponents charged him before Pilate with opposing Caesar (Luke 23:2). The closest link is thematic: God raises up servants to restore what is ruined, and the New Testament presents Jesus as the one in whom that restoration becomes complete.
questions: Nehemiah prayed for months and then prayed again in a single moment before answering the king. How do long seasons of prayer and quick prayers in the moment work together in your life?
Nehemiah surveyed the damage honestly before he said anything. Why is it important to see a problem clearly before calling others to fix it?
The people strengthened their hands for the good work despite mockery. What kind of ridicule or discouragement tends to stop you from starting something good?
